items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "Kekulé structure"?
options: A hydrocarbon containing one or more benzene rings.
A model of benzene as a ring of six carbon atoms with alternating C–C single and C=C double bonds.
The extra stability of benzene compared with the hypothetical Kekulé structure, shown by its less exothermic enthalpy change of hydrogenation.
A bond formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the plane of the bonded atoms.
items.answer: A model of benzene as a ring of six carbon atoms with alternating C–C single and C=C double bonds.
items.markingKey: Kekulé structure: a model of benzene as a ring of six carbon atoms with alternating C–C single and C=C double bonds.

items.stem: Why does benzene not decolourise bromine water, unlike cyclohexene?
options: Addition would destroy the stable delocalised π system
items.answer: Addition would destroy the stable delocalised π system
items.markingKey: Benzene prefers substitution.

items.stem: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of benzene is less exothermic than three times that of cyclohexene. This shows that
options: benzene is less stable than cyclohexene
benzene is more stable than the Kekulé structure suggests
items.answer: benzene is more stable than the Kekulé structure suggests
items.markingKey: Delocalisation energy.

items.stem: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −121 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene is −205 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the delocalisation (stabilisation) energy of benzene?
items.answer: 158 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: predicted = 3 × (−121) = −363 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]; stabilisation = −363 − (−205) = 158 kJ mol⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −121 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene is −207 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the predicted value for the Kekulé structure (cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene) and hence the stabilisation (delocalisation) energy of benzene. Write an equation for the hydrogenation of benzene and state the conditions.
items.answer: predicted −363 kJ mol⁻¹; stabilisation energy 156 kJ mol⁻¹; C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂ (Ni catalyst, heat, pressure)
items.markingKey: predicted = 3 × (−121) = −363 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]; stabilisation = −363 − (−207) = 156 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]; C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂ [1]; nickel catalyst, heat (about 150 °C), high pressure [1] [4]

items.stem: Isla compares cyclohexene and benzene. The enthalpy changes of hydrogenation are −120 kJ mol⁻¹ (cyclohexene) and −208 kJ mol⁻¹ (benzene). (a) Use the data to calculate the delocalisation energy of benzene. (b) Compare the reactions of cyclohexene and benzene with bromine at room temperature.
items.answer: (a) 152 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) Cyclohexene decolourises bromine rapidly by electrophilic addition; benzene does not react without a halogen carrier, and then undergoes substitution.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 × (−120) = −360 [1]; difference 152 kJ mol⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) cyclohexene addition [1]; benzene no reaction / substitution with catalyst [1] [2]

items.stem: What are the C–C–C bond angles in benzene?
items.markingKey: Planar hexagon, sp² carbons.

items.stem: Explain three pieces of evidence that the Kekulé structure of benzene is incorrect.
items.answer: All C–C bond lengths are equal (0.139 nm); enthalpy change of hydrogenation is about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic than predicted; benzene does not readily undergo addition (does not decolourise bromine water).
items.markingKey: bond lengths [1]; hydrogenation enthalpy [1]; lack of addition [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition reactions.
items.answer: Substitution keeps the delocalised π system and its stabilisation; addition would destroy it, which is energetically unfavourable.
items.markingKey: Substitution keeps the delocalised π system and its stabilisation [1]; addition would destroy it, which is energetically unfavourable [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why benzene is planar.
items.answer: Each carbon is sp² hybridised with three σ bonds at 120° in a plane; the p orbitals overlap best when the ring is flat.
items.markingKey: Each carbon is sp² hybridised with three σ bonds at 120° in a plane [1]; the p orbitals overlap best when the ring is flat [1] [2]

items.stem: Which observation about number of isomers is evidence against the Kekulé structure of benzene?
options: Benzene burns with a smoky flame
Benzene is a liquid at room temperature
items.answer: Only one 1,2-disubstituted benzene (e.g. 1,2-dibromobenzene) exists
items.markingKey: Only one 1,2-disubstituted benzene (e.g. 1,2-dibromobenzene) exists; Kekulé predicts two isomers (Br atoms across a single or a double bond).

items.stem: Which observation about bond lengths is evidence against the Kekulé structure of benzene?
options: X-ray diffraction shows all six C–C bonds are 0.139 nm, between C–C (0.154 nm) and C=C (0.134 nm)
Benzene burns with a smoky flame
Benzene is a liquid at room temperature
items.answer: X-ray diffraction shows all six C–C bonds are 0.139 nm, between C–C (0.154 nm) and C=C (0.134 nm)
items.markingKey: X-ray diffraction shows all six C–C bonds are 0.139 nm, between C–C (0.154 nm) and C=C (0.134 nm); Kekulé predicts alternating long and short bonds.

items.stem: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −118 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene is −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the predicted value for the Kekulé structure (cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene) and hence the stabilisation (delocalisation) energy of benzene. Write an equation for the hydrogenation of benzene and state the conditions. Explain what your answer shows about the structure of benzene.
items.answer: predicted −354 kJ mol⁻¹; stabilisation energy 146 kJ mol⁻¹; C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂ (Ni catalyst, heat, pressure); benzene is more stable than the Kekulé structure because its π electrons are delocalised
items.markingKey: predicted = 3 × (−118) = −354 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]; stabilisation = −354 − (−208) = 146 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]; C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂ [1]; nickel catalyst, heat (about 150 °C), high pressure [1]; benzene is more stable than Kekulé; delocalised π system [1] [5]

items.stem: Kenji compares cyclohexene and benzene. The enthalpy changes of hydrogenation are −119 kJ mol⁻¹ (cyclohexene) and −208 kJ mol⁻¹ (benzene). (a) Compare the reactions of cyclohexene and benzene with bromine at room temperature. (b) Explain why the π electrons in benzene are less available to electrophiles than those in cyclohexene.
items.answer: (a) Cyclohexene decolourises bromine rapidly by electrophilic addition; benzene does not react without a halogen carrier, and then undergoes substitution. (b) In benzene the π electrons are spread over six carbons (lower electron density) whereas in cyclohexene they are localised between two carbons (high electron density), so an electrophile is less strongly attracted/polarised.
items.markingKey: (a) cyclohexene addition [1]; benzene no reaction / substitution with catalyst [1] [2] (b) In benzene the π electrons are spread over six carbons (lower electron density) whereas in cyclohexene they are localised between two carbons (high electron density) [1]; so an electrophile is less strongly attracted/polarised [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the structure and bonding of benzene and evaluate the evidence that it is not adequately described by the Kekulé model.
items.answer: σ framework of sp² carbons, planar, 120°; overlapping p orbitals form delocalised π ring of six electrons; Kekulé: alternating single/double; evidence: equal bond lengths 0.139 nm, hydrogenation 152 kJ mol⁻¹ less exothermic, resistance to addition (bromine water), one 1,2-disubstituted isomer; consequence: substitution reactions preserve delocalisation.
items.markingKey: bonding description [2]; Kekulé model [1]; evidence (three pieces) [3]; consequence for reactivity [1] [7]

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "the alkylation or acylation of an arene using a halogenoalkane or acyl chloride with an AlCl₃ catalyst"?
items.answer: Friedel–Crafts reaction
items.markingKey: Friedel–Crafts reaction: the alkylation or acylation of an arene using a halogenoalkane or acyl chloride with an AlCl₃ catalyst.

items.stem: In the mechanism of nitration, what happens immediately after NO₂⁺ bonds to the ring?
options: An H⁺ is lost from the same carbon, restoring the delocalised system
A nucleophile adds to the ring
items.answer: An H⁺ is lost from the same carbon, restoring the delocalised system
items.markingKey: Intermediate loses H⁺.

items.stem: Why is the catalyst regenerated in the bromination of benzene?
options: H⁺ from the ring reacts with FeBr₄⁻ to form HBr and FeBr₃
FeBr₃ does not react at all
items.answer: H⁺ from the ring reacts with FeBr₄⁻ to form HBr and FeBr₃
items.markingKey: H⁺ + FeBr₄⁻ → FeBr₃ + HBr.

items.stem: Benzene is converted into methylbenzene by Friedel–Crafts alkylation. What is the electrophile?
items.answer: CH₃⁺
items.markingKey: CH₃Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃⁺ + AlCl₄⁻.

items.stem: Benzene is converted into methylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₃. Give the reagents and conditions, name the type of reaction, and write an equation for the formation of the electrophile.
items.answer: Chloromethane with an anhydrous aluminium chloride catalyst, heat under reflux; electrophilic substitution (Friedel–Crafts alkylation); CH₃Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃⁺ + AlCl₄⁻
items.markingKey: reagents [1]; conditions [1]; electrophilic substitution [1]; equation for electrophile [1] [4]

items.stem: Benzene is converted into methylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₃. Give the reagents and conditions, name the type of reaction, and write an equation for the formation of the electrophile. Describe the mechanism, using curly arrows in words.
items.answer: Chloromethane with an anhydrous aluminium chloride catalyst, heat under reflux; electrophilic substitution (Friedel–Crafts alkylation); CH₃Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃⁺ + AlCl₄⁻; mechanism: curly arrow from the π ring to CH₃⁺; positively charged intermediate (delocalisation partly lost); C–H bond breaks, electrons return to ring, H⁺ lost (forms HCl)
items.markingKey: reagents [1]; conditions [1]; electrophilic substitution [1]; equation for electrophile [1]; arrow from ring to electrophile [1]; intermediate with + charge [1]; loss of H⁺ restoring ring [1] [7]

items.stem: Sipho plans to make ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, from benzene in a school laboratory by Friedel–Crafts alkylation. (a) State the reagents and conditions needed. (b) Write an equation to show how the electrophile is formed. (c) Explain why the reaction gives a substitution product rather than an addition product.
items.answer: (a) Chloroethane with an anhydrous aluminium chloride catalyst, heat under reflux (b) CH₃CH₂Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CH₂⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ (c) Loss of H⁺ restores the stable delocalised π system; addition would destroy it.
items.markingKey: (a) reagents [1]; conditions [1] [2] (b) CH₃CH₂Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CH₂⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ [1] (c) Loss of H⁺ restores the stable delocalised π system; addition would destroy it [1]

items.stem: Aisha plans to make chlorobenzene, C₆H₅Cl, from benzene in a university teaching laboratory by chlorination. (a) Write an equation to show how the electrophile is formed. (b) Describe the mechanism of the reaction. (c) Explain why the reaction gives a substitution product rather than an addition product.
items.answer: (a) Cl₂ + AlCl₃ → Cl⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ (b) π electrons of the ring attack Cl⁺; arenium (positive) intermediate forms with delocalisation partly lost; C–H bond breaks and electrons return to the ring, restoring delocalisation; H⁺ lost. (c) Loss of H⁺ restores the stable delocalised π system; addition would destroy it.
items.markingKey: (a) Cl₂ + AlCl₃ → Cl⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ [1] (b) attack by ring [1]; intermediate [1]; H⁺ lost / ring restored [1] [3] (c) Loss of H⁺ restores the stable delocalised π system; addition would destroy it [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "arenium intermediate"?
options: A species that accepts a pair of electrons to form a new covalent bond.
A reaction in which an electrophile replaces a hydrogen atom on an arene ring.
A Lewis acid catalyst such as FeBr₃ or AlCl₃ that polarises a halogen molecule to generate the electrophile.
The positively charged intermediate formed when an electrophile bonds to a benzene ring, in which delocalisation is partly lost.
items.answer: The positively charged intermediate formed when an electrophile bonds to a benzene ring, in which delocalisation is partly lost.
items.markingKey: Arenium intermediate: the positively charged intermediate formed when an electrophile bonds to a benzene ring, in which delocalisation is partly lost.

items.stem: Describe the mechanism of the bromination of benzene.
items.answer: FeBr₃ polarises Br₂ forming Br⁺ (FeBr₄⁻); π electrons of the ring attack Br⁺ forming a positive intermediate with partly broken delocalisation; C–H bond breaks, electrons return to the ring, H⁺ lost; H⁺ + FeBr₄⁻ → HBr + FeBr₃.
items.markingKey: electrophile formation [1]; curly arrow from ring to Br⁺ [1]; intermediate [1]; loss of H⁺ and catalyst regenerated [1] [4]

items.stem: Explain why the temperature is kept below 55 °C in the nitration of benzene.
items.answer: Above this, further substitution occurs to give dinitro (and trinitro) products.
items.markingKey: Above this, further substitution occurs to give dinitro (and trinitro) products [1]

items.stem: Explain why the side chain of methylbenzene reacts with chlorine in UV light but the ring reacts with chlorine in the presence of AlCl₃.
items.answer: UV light produces Cl radicals that substitute H on the CH₃ group (free-radical substitution); AlCl₃ generates the electrophile Cl⁺, which substitutes on the electron-rich ring (electrophilic substitution).
items.markingKey: UV: free-radical on side chain [1]; AlCl₃: electrophilic on ring [1] [2]

items.stem: Chloe writes in a revision note: "Friedel–Crafts reactions can be carried out in aqueous solution." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: AlCl₃ reacts with water, so anhydrous conditions are needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: AlCl₃ reacts with water, so anhydrous conditions are needed. [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "phenol"?
options: An acid that only partly dissociates in water, such as phenol (Ka about 1.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ mol dm⁻³).
C₆H₅O⁻, the anion formed when phenol loses H⁺; its negative charge is delocalised into the ring.
The white precipitate formed when phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature.
C₆H₅OH, a compound in which an –OH group is bonded directly to a benzene ring.
items.answer: C₆H₅OH, a compound in which an –OH group is bonded directly to a benzene ring.
items.markingKey: Phenol: C₆H₅OH, a compound in which an –OH group is bonded directly to a benzene ring.

items.stem: Why does phenol react with bromine water without a catalyst, unlike benzene?
options: A lone pair on O is delocalised into the ring, increasing its electron density
items.answer: A lone pair on O is delocalised into the ring, increasing its electron density
items.markingKey: Activated ring polarises Br₂.

items.stem: Why is phenol more acidic than ethanol?
options: The negative charge of the phenoxide ion is delocalised over the ring
The ethoxide ion is stabilised by its alkyl group
Phenol is more soluble in water
items.answer: The negative charge of the phenoxide ion is delocalised over the ring
items.markingKey: Stabilised conjugate base.

Ravi is given three colourless liquids labelled A, B and C. They are ethanol, phenol (dissolved in water) and ethanoic acid, but the labels have been lost. pKa values: ethanol about 16, phenol 9.9, ethanoic acid 4.8. (a) Describe a test that distinguishes phenol from ethanol, giving the equation. (b) Explain why phenol undergoes substitution with bromine more readily than benzene.
items.answer: (a) Bromine water: phenol decolourises it with a white precipitate (C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr); ethanol no change. (b) Lone pair on O delocalised into the ring increases electron density, polarising Br₂ without a catalyst.
items.markingKey: (a) test and observations [1]; equation [1] [2] (b) Lone pair on O delocalised into the ring increases electron density [1]; polarising Br₂ without a catalyst [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the order of acidity, weakest first?
items.answer: Ethanol < water < phenol
items.markingKey: Phenoxide is stabilised by delocalisation; ethoxide destabilised by alkyl group.

items.stem: Explain why phenol is a stronger acid than ethanol.
items.answer: In the phenoxide ion, a lone pair on oxygen overlaps with the π system so the negative charge is delocalised over the ring, stabilising the ion; in ethoxide the alkyl group pushes electron density onto O⁻, destabilising it. So phenol dissociates more.
items.markingKey: phenoxide charge delocalised [1]; ethoxide destabilised by alkyl group [1]; more dissociation [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why phenol reacts more readily than benzene with electrophiles.
items.answer: A lone pair from the oxygen is partially delocalised into the ring, increasing the π electron density so the ring polarises electrophiles more easily; substitution occurs at the 2-, 4- and 6- positions.
items.markingKey: lone pair delocalised into ring [1]; higher electron density [1]; 2,4,6 positions [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how phenol can be distinguished from ethanol using a chemical test.
items.answer: Add bromine water: phenol decolourises it and gives a white precipitate; ethanol gives no change. (Or: phenol gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃.)
items.markingKey: test [1]; results for both [1] [2]

items.stem: What is formed when phenol reacts with aqueous sodium carbonate?

items.answer: No reaction (phenol is too weak an acid)
items.markingKey: no reaction; no effervescence.

items.stem: Describe what is observed when phenol is added to dilute nitric acid at room temperature. Name the organic product and write an equation.
items.answer: A mixture of yellow 2- and 4-nitrophenol forms; 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol; C₆H₅OH + HNO₃ → HOC₆H₄NO₂ + H₂O
items.markingKey: observation [1]; product [1]; equation [1] [3]

items.stem: Compare the acidity of phenol with that of water, ethanol and ethanoic acid, and describe the reactions of phenol with sodium, sodium hydroxide and bromine water.
items.answer: Order ethanol < water < phenol < ethanoic acid; phenoxide stabilised by delocalisation; alkoxide destabilised by +I alkyl; carboxylate charge over two O; Na gives H₂ and sodium phenoxide; NaOH gives sodium phenoxide (no reaction with carbonate); bromine water gives white 2,4,6-tribromophenol – activated ring; equations.
items.markingKey: acidity order [1]; explanation [2]; sodium [1]; NaOH and carbonate [1]; bromine water with explanation [2] [7]

items.stem: Grace is given three colourless liquids labelled A, B and C. They are ethanol, phenol (dissolved in water) and ethanoic acid, but the labels have been lost. pKa values: ethanol about 16, phenol 9.9, ethanoic acid 4.8. (a) Describe a test that distinguishes phenol from ethanol, giving the equation. (b) Explain why phenol reacts with sodium hydroxide but ethanol does not.
items.answer: (a) Bromine water: phenol decolourises it with a white precipitate (C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr); ethanol no change. (b) Phenol is acidic enough (pKa 9.9) to be deprotonated by OH⁻; ethanol is a weaker acid than water, so the equilibrium lies to the left.
items.markingKey: (a) test and observations [1]; equation [1] [2] (b) Phenol is acidic enough (pKa 9.9) to be deprotonated by OH⁻ [1]; ethanol is a weaker acid than water, so the equilibrium lies to the left [1] [2]

items.stem: Mateo is given three colourless liquids labelled A, B and C. They are ethanol, phenol (dissolved in water) and ethanoic acid, but the labels have been lost. pKa values: ethanol about 16, phenol 9.9, ethanoic acid 4.8. (a) Place the three compounds in order of increasing acidity and explain the position of phenol. (b) Describe a test that distinguishes phenol from ethanol, giving the equation.
items.answer: (a) Ethanol < phenol < ethanoic acid; phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge into the ring, but less than the carboxylate ion, where the charge is delocalised over two electronegative O atoms. (b) Bromine water: phenol decolourises it with a white precipitate (C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr); ethanol no change.
items.markingKey: (a) order [1]; phenoxide delocalisation [1]; comparison with carboxylate [1] [3] (b) test and observations [1]; equation [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "deactivating group"?

A substituent that directs incoming electrophiles to the 3- position, e.g. –NO₂, –COOH, –CHO, –COR.
A substituent that directs incoming electrophiles to the 2- and 4- positions, e.g. –OH, –NH₂, –CH₃, –Cl.

items.stem: Predict the main organic product(s) of the nitration of nitrobenzene (concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄, heat above 55 °C). Explain your answer in terms of the directing effect of the substituent.
items.answer: 1,3-dinitrobenzene; –NO₂ is 3-directing and deactivating (electron-withdrawing)
items.markingKey: product(s) [1]; directing effect of the substituent [1] [2]

items.stem: How many electrons are in the delocalised π system of benzene?
items.markingKey: One p electron from each carbon.

items.stem: A student in Madrid states: "Benzene has alternating single and double bonds of different lengths." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: All six C–C bonds are the same length, 0.139 nm.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: All six C–C bonds are the same length, 0.139 nm. [2]

items.stem: The enthalpy change of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −119 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene is −207 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the delocalisation (stabilisation) energy of benzene?
items.answer: 150 kJ mol⁻¹
items.markingKey: predicted = 3 × (−119) = −357 kJ mol⁻¹ [1]; stabilisation = −357 − (−207) = 150 kJ mol⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe and explain two pieces of evidence, one involving reaction with bromine and one involving number of isomers, that show benzene does not have the Kekulé structure.
items.answer: Benzene does not decolourise bromine water at room temperature (Kekulé predicts rapid electrophilic addition like an alkene); only one 1,2-disubstituted benzene (e.g. 1,2-dibromobenzene) exists (Kekulé predicts two isomers (Br atoms across a single or a double bond)). Both show the π electrons are delocalised.
items.markingKey: first evidence [1]; contrast with Kekulé prediction [1]; second evidence [1]; contrast [1] [4]

items.stem: Mateo compares cyclohexene and benzene. The enthalpy changes of hydrogenation are −120 kJ mol⁻¹ (cyclohexene) and −208 kJ mol⁻¹ (benzene). (a) Use the data to calculate the delocalisation energy of benzene. (b) Explain why the π electrons in benzene are less available to electrophiles than those in cyclohexene.
items.answer: (a) 152 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) In benzene the π electrons are spread over six carbons (lower electron density) whereas in cyclohexene they are localised between two carbons (high electron density), so an electrophile is less strongly attracted/polarised.
items.markingKey: (a) 3 × (−120) = −360 [1]; difference 152 kJ mol⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) In benzene the π electrons are spread over six carbons (lower electron density) whereas in cyclohexene they are localised between two carbons (high electron density) [1]; so an electrophile is less strongly attracted/polarised [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the electrophile in the nitration of benzene?
items.answer: NO₂⁺
items.markingKey: Nitronium ion.

items.stem: A student in Dhaka states: "Friedel–Crafts reactions can be carried out in aqueous solution." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: AlCl₃ reacts with water, so anhydrous conditions are needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: AlCl₃ reacts with water, so anhydrous conditions are needed. [2]

items.answer: FeBr₃ is regenerated when H⁺ reacts with FeBr₄⁻, so it is a catalyst.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: FeBr₃ is regenerated when H⁺ reacts with FeBr₄⁻, so it is a catalyst. [2]

items.stem: 3.90 g of benzene (Mr 78.0) was converted into phenylethanone (Mr 120.0) by Friedel–Crafts acylation. The mass of purified phenylethanone obtained was 3.72 g. What is the percentage yield?
Which reagents and conditions convert benzene into ethylbenzene?
options: Chlorine with an aluminium chloride (or iron(III) chloride) catalyst, room temperature, dry
Chloroethane with an anhydrous aluminium chloride catalyst, heat under reflux
Concentrated nitric acid and concentrated sulfuric acid, below 55 °C
Bromine with an iron(III) bromide (or iron) catalyst, room temperature, dry
items.answer: Chloroethane with an anhydrous aluminium chloride catalyst, heat under reflux
items.markingKey: Friedel–Crafts alkylation: chloroethane with an anhydrous aluminium chloride catalyst, heat under reflux.

items.stem: Kwame plans to make phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃, from benzene in a university teaching laboratory by Friedel–Crafts acylation. (a) Describe the mechanism of the reaction. (b) Explain why the reaction gives a substitution product rather than an addition product.
items.answer: (a) π electrons of the ring attack CH₃CO⁺; arenium (positive) intermediate forms with delocalisation partly lost; C–H bond breaks and electrons return to the ring, restoring delocalisation; H⁺ lost. (b) Loss of H⁺ restores the stable delocalised π system; addition would destroy it.
items.markingKey: (a) attack by ring [1]; intermediate [1]; H⁺ lost / ring restored [1] [3] (b) Loss of H⁺ restores the stable delocalised π system; addition would destroy it [1]

items.stem: Daniel plans to make phenylethanone, C₆H₅COCH₃, from benzene in a university teaching laboratory by Friedel–Crafts acylation. (a) State the reagents and conditions needed. (b) Write an equation to show how the electrophile is formed. (c) Describe the mechanism of the reaction.
items.answer: (a) Ethanoyl chloride with an anhydrous aluminium chloride catalyst, heat under reflux (b) CH₃COCl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CO⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ (c) π electrons of the ring attack CH₃CO⁺; arenium (positive) intermediate forms with delocalisation partly lost; C–H bond breaks and electrons return to the ring, restoring delocalisation; H⁺ lost.

items.answer: Activating group

items.stem: A student in Madrid states: "Phenol reacts with sodium carbonate to give carbon dioxide." Explain why this statement is incorrect.

items.stem: 1.88 g of phenol (Mr 94.0) was treated with excess bromine water. What is the theoretical mass of 2,4,6-tribromophenol (Mr 330.7) that could be formed?
Describe what is observed when phenol is added to sodium metal. Name the organic product and write an equation.
items.answer: Effervescence; sodium dissolves; sodium phenoxide and hydrogen; 2C₆H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₆H₅ONa + H₂
items.markingKey: observation [1]; product [1]; equation [1] [3]

items.stem: Diego is given three colourless liquids labelled A, B and C. They are ethanol, phenol (dissolved in water) and ethanoic acid, but the labels have been lost. pKa values: ethanol about 16, phenol 9.9, ethanoic acid 4.8. (a) Place the three compounds in order of increasing acidity and explain the position of phenol. (b) Explain why phenol reacts with sodium hydroxide but ethanol does not.
items.answer: (a) Ethanol < phenol < ethanoic acid; phenoxide ion is stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge into the ring, but less than the carboxylate ion, where the charge is delocalised over two electronegative O atoms. (b) Phenol is acidic enough (pKa 9.9) to be deprotonated by OH⁻; ethanol is a weaker acid than water, so the equilibrium lies to the left.
items.markingKey: (a) order [1]; phenoxide delocalisation [1]; comparison with carboxylate [1] [3] (b) Phenol is acidic enough (pKa 9.9) to be deprotonated by OH⁻ [1]; ethanol is a weaker acid than water, so the equilibrium lies to the left [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why methylbenzene undergoes nitration faster than benzene.
items.answer: The methyl group donates electron density into the ring (positive inductive effect), increasing the π electron density so the ring attracts the electrophile NO₂⁺ more strongly and the intermediate is stabilised.
items.markingKey: electron-donating CH₃ [1]; higher ring electron density / intermediate stabilised [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the order of steps matters when making a disubstituted benzene.
items.answer: The first substituent controls where the second goes: a 2,4-directing group gives 2- and 4- products, a 3-directing group gives 3- products, so the steps must be ordered to give the required isomer.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: The first substituent controls where the second goes: a 2,4-directing group gives 2- and 4- products; a 3-directing group gives 3- products; so the steps must be ordered to give the required isomer (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: In the nitration of methylbenzene (concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄, about 30 °C), at which position(s) on the ring does substitution mainly occur?
items.answer: the 2- and 4- positions
items.markingKey: –CH₃ is 2,4-directing: 2-nitromethylbenzene and 4-nitromethylbenzene.

items.stem: What is the length of the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene compared with C–C (0.154 nm) and C=C (0.134 nm)?
items.answer: All 0.139 nm, between the two

Benzene burns with a smoky flame
Benzene is a liquid at room temperature
items.answer: Benzene does not decolourise bromine water at room temperature

items.stem: Describe and explain two pieces of evidence, one involving enthalpy of hydrogenation and one involving bond lengths, that show benzene does not have the Kekulé structure.
items.answer: Hydrogenation of benzene releases about 152 kJ mol⁻¹ less energy than three times that of cyclohexene (Kekulé predicts about −360 kJ mol⁻¹); X-ray diffraction shows all six C–C bonds are 0.139 nm, between C–C (0.154 nm) and C=C (0.134 nm) (Kekulé predicts alternating long and short bonds). Both show the π electrons are delocalised.
items.markingKey: first evidence [1]; contrast with Kekulé prediction [1]; second evidence [1]; contrast [1] [4]

items.stem: Hana compares cyclohexene and benzene. The enthalpy changes of hydrogenation are −119 kJ mol⁻¹ (cyclohexene) and −208 kJ mol⁻¹ (benzene). (a) Use the data to calculate the delocalisation energy of benzene. (b) Compare the reactions of cyclohexene and benzene with bromine at room temperature.
items.answer: (a) 149 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) Cyclohexene decolourises bromine rapidly by electrophilic addition; benzene does not react without a halogen carrier, and then undergoes substitution.

items.stem: Hana plans to make methylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₃, from benzene in a college laboratory by Friedel–Crafts alkylation. (a) Write an equation to show how the electrophile is formed. (b) Explain why benzene needs a catalyst for this reaction whereas an alkene does not. (c) Explain why the reaction gives a substitution product rather than an addition product.
items.answer: (a) CH₃Cl + AlCl₃ → CH₃⁺ + AlCl₄⁻ (b) Benzene's π electrons are delocalised (lower electron density) so it cannot polarise the reagent; a strong electrophile must be generated by the catalyst. (c) Loss of H⁺ restores the stable delocalised π system; addition would destroy it.
